Title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-scorpion-toxin-binder-design

Published Time: 2026-10-20T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
_**Summary:**As part of our work experimenting with how Claude can help accelerate drug discovery, we asked an internal research model to design_ minibinders _(small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins. Claude worked from our prompt and four follow-ups, which we developed in collaboration with the financial investment research firm Citrini Research. Teams at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience experimentally tested 211 designs for binding. Of these, 17 met our criteria. We’re releasing all 211 designs and their data as a resource for the field._

In August, we showed [how Claude designed protein minibinders](https://www.anthropic.com/research/Claude-accelerates-protein-design) after being given a single prompt. A month before we released those results, a team from [Citrini Research](https://www.citriniresearch.com/) had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? Members of our life science research team set out to answer this, first by brainstorming problems with Claude. We landed on asking for Claude’s help designing novel protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that they could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom.

Scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more every year, resulting in more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in parts of the world with limited access to medical care. New treatments are expensive to make, and are also unlikely to earn back the cost of developing them. With so little investment, scorpion envenomation has been [described as](https://gh.bmj.com/content/10/11/e020682) a neglected tropical disease.

We started by giving Claude the same prompt we’d used in our earlier protein-binder study, after modifying it with Citrini.[1](https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-scorpion-toxin-binder-design#footnote-1) Over the next 64 hours, an internal research model, operating within Claude Science, worked mainly autonomously, although we directed its work with four follow-ups. Under our supervision, Claude analyzed the research data, generated the figures, and drafted the final report.

Claude’s design campaign produced 17 protein binders that each bind to one of four scorpion neurotoxins that are known to be dangerous to humans. Throughout the process, Claude generated 318,484 protein designs and selected 180 of them for testing. Our team added 31 more, with Claude’s help. Our partners at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, two contract research organizations (CROs), lab-tested all 211 designs to see if they would bind to the toxins they were designed against, and 17 designs met our criteria for a binder. We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so we do not claim to have produced an antivenom.

We sent Claude’s work to two outside experts, Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins, who said they felt this work was a promising first step. If AI can now design credible binders against several hard-to-target toxins in days and they can be confirmed in the lab within weeks, this could, in theory, speed up discovery for envenomation and other neglected diseases. The challenge, as always, is turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs.

We share more detail in our [technical report](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/31ac578806cffd8b3d92d8affe6edc4c04d502e1.pdf), and are making [all 211 designs and their data available](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Anthropic/scorpion-toxin-binder-design).

> Designing a binder against almost any target no longer seems unrealistic. We can now obtain very tight binders remarkably quickly, and binding itself is no longer the main bottleneck. For venomous animals such as snakes and scorpions, whose bites and stings kill or seriously injure large numbers of people, particularly in underserved regions, the real impact will come from tackling the parts of the therapeutic pipeline that go beyond binding. The challenge is to use these extraordinary tools to develop molecules that can become real drugs, ones that are safe, affordable, and widely accessible.

_**Susana Vázquez Torres**, Postdoctoral Researcher, Structural Biology Programme, Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO), Madrid, Spain._

### Designing _de novo_ binders against five toxins from four species of scorpions

Scorpion venom contains multiple protein neurotoxins. The neurotoxins that are most likely to harm or kill humans attach to _sodium channels_, large proteins embedded in the membranes of nerve cells that allow them to fire. When sodium channels are disrupted, nerves fire at the wrong time—this releases large amounts of stress chemicals, like adrenaline. In severe cases, this can cause heart failure and excess fluid buildup in the lungs, occasionally resulting in death.

There are some antivenoms available for scorpion stings. They’re generally made using the antibodies of immunized animals, a process that can take months. Venom is milked from thousands of scorpions and used to immunize horses; scientists then purify the resulting antibodies from the horses’ blood. Traditional antivenoms can work when given early, but they’re usually effective for only a small number of neurotoxins. They’re also expensive to produce, and in many regions are costly or in short supply.

_De novo_ design offers a potential solution. A binder is a molecule that attaches tightly to a specific target; antibodies are one natural example. In principle, a binder that targets the part of a neurotoxin that latches onto sodium channels could stop the toxin from reaching the channel. In _de novo_ design, protein binders are generated from scratch against a specific target. These binders are designed computationally and can be optimized for druglike properties such as potency and stability, which could make them easier to supply in regions where stings most often occur.

Our approach was inspired by [an earlier effort](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08393-x) that designed _de novo_ proteins that neutralized snake neurotoxins and protected mice. To our knowledge, no _de novo_-designed binders against scorpion neurotoxins have been described.

For this campaign, we chose to target five scorpion-venom neurotoxins across four regions: Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II), and the Middle East (LqhIII). We also chose to aim the designs at each toxin’s channel-binding site. Claude picked the toxin structures to use for design by searching the Protein Data Bank (PDB) as well as the AlphaFold database (AFDB). For each toxin, it selected five _hotspots_, specific amino acid positions on the toxin that its binder designs were meant to latch onto.

We were primarily wondering if Claude could design binders against _individual_ toxins. But we were also curious if Claude could design binders that targeted _multiple_ toxins. There’s a practical reason for trying to design multitoxin binders, namely that it would reduce the number of molecules needed for a universal antivenom cocktail—which would be the most cost-effective and regionally neutral treatment. We selected these five scorpion toxins (Cn2, Ts1, AaH I, AaH II, and LqhIII) as a challenging test of multitoxin design: they share one fold for the overall shape of the protein, but any two are only 26% to 62% identical in their amino acid sequences.

To see how far Claude could go, we asked it to design four kinds of binders: binders against each of the five toxins individually; binders that targeted the β-family toxins Ts1 and Cn2; binders that targeted the α-family toxins AaH II, AaH I, and LqhIII; and binders that targeted all five toxins simultaneously.

> Designing credible binders against five toxins in parallel, in a matter of days, is a great showcase of the AI-driven paradigm shift we are seeing in therapeutic discovery. This is especially true for neglected diseases such as animal envenomings, which have been largely starved of innovation due to low commercial incentives. Being able to agentically tackle the uniquely broad target space across animal toxins provides a significant speed-up in discovery, and brings realistic therapeutic solutions much closer.

_**Timothy P. Jenkins**, Associate Professor, Technical University of Denmark._

#### Claude ran the design campaign with considerable autonomy

Our initial prompt defined the neurotoxin targets, the protein design and folding tools, and the rules for novelty, scoring, and filtering. Beyond choosing the structures and amino acid hotspots, Claude also set the quality thresholds a design had to clear, decided how much to lean on each available design tool, and developed the strategies for designing binders against multiple toxins.

Ultimately, Claude used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 designs, filtering out any that resembled a toxin or a known protein. Claude co-folded and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs, predicting each pair’s structure as one complex. Sixty-four hours after we gave Claude our initial prompt, it produced its final list of 180 designs. The campaign used on the order of 10,000 GPU hours.[2](https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-scorpion-toxin-binder-design#footnote-2)

Claude worked autonomously for 24 hours following our first prompt. Its results encouraged us to prompt Claude to continue its campaign and look for better designs. Our follow-up prompts were mainly focused on directing Claude to design a multitoxin binder. Claude selected most of the 180 designs—including our strongest binder (Cn2-B1)—only after our third follow-up. At our request, Claude sent the protein sequences to Twist Bioscience (in emails indicating they were written by Claude), which produced the proteins in order to see how well they would bind to the toxins. We later worked with Claude to add another 31 designs, increasing the total to 211 designs: 60 designs against a single toxin (12 per toxin), 30 designs against the two β-family toxins, 30 designs against the three α-family toxins, and 91 designs against all five toxins.

Of the 211 designs our teams assessed, 17 met our criteria for a binder, each against a single toxin. None of the designs made against multiple toxins met our criteria for more than one. (Beyond being limited by its current capabilities, there could be many explanations for why Claude struggled with this, including our prompting, the limitations of available design tools, and even the biological feasibility of multitoxin design.) Seven designs were binders against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I, and two against LqhIII. Among the 60 single-toxin designs, 11 were binders (18%). This rate is consistent with typical protein design campaigns, including our previous work.

#### Testing Claude's designs in the lab

After completing the campaign, we sent the designs to Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience to test them for binding. Each group produced the designs in their labs, but in different formats. Adaptyv Bio expressed them in a _cell-free system_, which uses protein-making machinery extracted from bacteria rather than living cells. Twist Bioscience expressed the designs in mammalian cells (in this case, human kidney cells) as fusions to _Fc_, the stem of an antibody. These are complementary ways to measure the underlying binding process, and we combined them in order to improve confidence in our results.

Title: GitHub - AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor: AI mentor that corrects your written math visually with local harnesses.

URL Source: https://github.com/AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor

Markdown Content:
A maths mentor at the tip of your pen. Press a key while you work by hand: Claude, Gemini or GPT marks your work on the
 screen like a teacher with coloured pens, gives you hints instead of answers, and shows the idea as a 3Blue1Brown-style animation.

Handwriting in xournal++ → one key → the slip is marked on the page → box the integral → an interactive manim animation. ([video](https://github.com/AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor/blob/main/docs/demo.mp4); for a repeatable recording the pen is scripted and the model's answer is a fixed example.)

## Why I use it

I study calculus with a pen tablet in xournal++. I kept screenshotting my work into Claude and reading long answers back, when what I wanted was a teacher looking over my shoulder: circle the mistake, tick what's right, nudge me toward the next step, and _show_ me why. penmentor is that, one key away, on my own Claude subscription.

## How it helps you learn

*   **Hints, not answers.** A ladder from a nudge to naming the technique to a faint ghost of the next line: you do the thinking, which is what makes it stick.
*   **Feedback on your own work.** The first real mistake circled where you made it, correct lines ticked, later lines that inherit the mistake underlined. The marks stay while you keep writing; Esc clears them.
*   **Practice that makes you recall.** Questions on your key steps (answer by typing or by writing), find-the-error drills, "which technique fits?".
*   **See it.** Box what you want to understand and get an interactive animation made with 3Blue1Brown's own [manim](https://github.com/3b1b/manim): drag the bounds, retype a value, watch Riemann sums close in.
*   **Whole page aware.** A small xournal++ plugin shares the page you are on, not just what fits on screen.

## Works with Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity

penmentor runs on the AI command-line agent you already use, on that subscription. Pick the model in _Settings_; its prefix says which agent answers:

| Prefix | Agent | For example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `claude:` | [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) | `claude:opus`, `claude:sonnet`, `claude:haiku` |
| `codex:` | [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) | `codex:gpt-5.6-terra` |
| `agy:` | Antigravity CLI | `agy:gemini-4-argon-medium`, `agy:gemini-3.8-flash-medium` |

Settings lists the agents you have installed. How each one is run and what it sees: [the guide](https://github.com/AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor/blob/main/docs/guide.md#how-it-works-and-what-leaves-your-computer).

## Quick start

git clone https://github.com/AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor ~/src/penmentor
~/src/penmentor/bin/penmentor --selftest

Linux on X11 (best with i3), with one of those agents logged in (`claude`, `codex` or `agy`), plus `rofi`, `slop`, `xdotool` and PyQt6. Bind `bin/penmentor` to a key ([example](https://github.com/AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor/blob/main/contrib/i3.conf)). Setup, keys and how it works: [the guide](https://github.com/AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor/blob/main/docs/guide.md).

Title: Franchisee reconciles cash in 94% less time with ChatGPT Work

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/ted-taylor-restaurant

Markdown Content:
Ted Taylor entered the restaurant business after a 25-year career in the semiconductor industry. Today, he’s an independent franchisee operating three co-branded Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon restaurants across New Mexico.

Running quick-service restaurants means balancing the customer experience with a lot of work customers never see, like menu pricing, staffing, equipment maintenance, and policies. Ted uses OpenAI technology to get through all of it faster.

With ChatGPT, Ted accelerates time-consuming tasks like research and drafting, and he uses ChatGPT Work to gather and analyze volumes of data across pricing, sales, forecasts, schedules, and labor and to get recommendations on where each restaurant needs attention, reducing repricing time by 95% and shaving 4 hours off payroll runs.

> “ChatGPT Work’s recommendations are so good that it’s much faster to start there and then make adjustments.”

—Ted Taylor, independent franchisee, Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon

## Repricing menus across three markets in minutes

Repricing menus is an annual undertaking that requires a complex analysis of recipe costs, item popularity, local competitor pricing, portion sizes, and the different economics of in-store and delivery orders. Ted uses ChatGPT Work to bring those factors together and get pricing recommendations in 1 - 2 hours instead of 5 days.

> “It used to take me a few days of work to analyze and come up with item-level pricing; whereas, ChatGPT Work tears through it in a matter of moments and does it more thoroughly.”

—Ted Taylor, independent franchisee, Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon

Ted first uses ChatGPT Work to research and establish his pricing targets and pricing strategies based on local competitors’ pricing trends, portion sizes, and relative food quality. He then gives ChatGPT Work a categorized list of menu items with their current in-store and delivery prices. He specifies how much he wants each set of prices to increase overall and which items should receive larger or smaller increases, largely based on the earlier analysis from ChatGPT.

He can make the analysis more detailed by adding item-level sales history and supplier prices. ChatGPT Work can use these inputs to estimate sales impacts from price changes and to optimize item-level pricing around cost of goods targets.

ChatGPT Work returns a spreadsheet with recommended in-store and delivery prices. It will even relate the pricing changes to an overall pricing strategy designed to optimize business outcomes like customer retention, minimizing price shocks, and best positioning of add-ons.

The first time Ted used ChatGPT Work for pricing, he also ran the analysis manually. “ChatGPT Work made a deeper local comparison and helped me avoid increases that would have made some items uncompetitive,” he said. Ted immediately switched to using ChatGPT to develop the first recommendations.

## Finding ways to optimize labor and free up cash flow

Ted uses ChatGPT Work to help manage labor costs in two ways: reviewing how labor is tracking across his three restaurants and testing a better way to build the weekly schedule.

For the labor analysis, Ted gave ChatGPT Work read-only access to his sales and labor data. When he runs the analysis, it compares scheduled, budgeted, and actual hours with forecast and actual sales. It also reviews the previous 12 weeks to account for stores that routinely come in above or below their sales forecasts. The resulting report flags overtime, shifts running longer than planned, and gaps in coverage, and highlights what a manager should review.

For the scheduling test, Ted gave ChatGPT Work an employee roster with each person’s role, training, availability, and pay, along with the store’s staffing needs at different sales levels. He and the manager compared ChatGPT Work’s proposed schedule with what she would have built, identified missing rules about when to add staff during busy periods, and refined the instructions for ChatGPT Work.

ChatGPT Work now produces a full schedule for that location. The manager checks it over, makes adjustments if needed, and enters it into the restaurant’s scheduling system. Ted estimates that better scheduling could eventually reduce hourly labor costs by one to two percentage points of sales across all three restaurants, which could add $50,000 to $100,000 in free cash flow annually that can be utilized for increased pay, bonuses, investment in the business, or increased profit distributions.

## Accelerating back-office tasks with ChatGPT Work

Ted also uses ChatGPT Work for day-to-day operations, from developing HR policies to reconciling cash and managing supply and repair requests.

When New Mexico started requiring restaurants to keep a written procedure for bodily-fluid incidents, Ted used ChatGPT to write a draft in about 30 seconds. When Ted needed a social media policy for his employee handbook, ChatGPT helped him quickly draft guidance that an outside HR firm later reviewed without making any changes.

Ted uses ChatGPT Work to reconcile cash monthly across his three restaurants. He uploads each store’s cash transaction data and bank records, and ChatGPT Work compares the transactions with the corresponding deposits. Monthly reconciliation used to take three hours, and now it takes 5-10 minutes. He also cut four hours of manual work from every payroll cycle by using ChatGPT Work to summarize payroll inputs.

To help keep restaurants running smoothly, Ted also used ChatGPT Work to build a web portal where employees can request supplies or repairs. The portal notifies him through a dedicated email address and tracks each request’s status.

## More time to improve the business, not just run it

Ted’s approach to using ChatGPT Work is practical for any small-business owner. He gives ChatGPT the same data and guidelines he’d use to make a decision and compares its output with how he’d do the work himself. As he gains confidence in the results, he expands his use to more tasks around the business, always reviewing the results before implementing.

For Ted, the value of ChatGPT Work goes beyond hours saved. Now he can do analysis he might otherwise skip and spend more time on customers, employees, and growing the business.

articles.content:
Title: GitHub - deepseek-ai/DeepInfer: DeepInfer: High-performance, large-scale inference framework for DeepSeek models

URL Source: https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer

Markdown Content:
DeepInfer is the high-performance inference framework that powers DeepSeek's large-scale production services. This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale.

Supported models:

*   DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Supported features:

*   Optimized kernels, model and sampler runtime
*   Parallelism: Attention DP / balanced CP, MoE EP + EPLB
*   DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification
*   SWA bounded replay
*   Asynchronous scheduling (zero-overhead batch scheduler)
*   Batch-invariant inference
*   Deterministic sampling
*   Structured outputs

Feature details and configuration
*   **Optimized kernels:**[FlashMLA](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/FlashMLA), [DeepGEMM](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM), [DeepEP](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP), [TileKernels](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/TileKernels), [DeepSelect](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSelect), and custom [TileLang kernels](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/deepinfer/model_executor/layers/tilelang_ops).
*   **DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification:** accelerate decoding with draft tokens and use confidence estimates to schedule verification. Set `DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1`; `DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE` controls the maximum draft length (default: 5).
*   **Decoder SWA bounded replay:** reduce decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix. Set `DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact` and `DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140` for the default V4.1 settings; the retained suffix must cover the SWA window plus the maximum backtracking length.
*   **Asynchronous scheduling:** overlap CPU batch scheduling with device execution. Enabled by default.
*   **Batch-invariant inference:** keep model results identical across different batch compositions. Enable with `DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` (NVIDIA only).
*   **Deterministic sampling:** produce identical outputs for identical input tokens and sampling parameters. Set `DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0` and pass a fixed `seq_seed` to `SamplingParams` (NVIDIA only).
*   **Structured outputs:** constrain generation to a regex, JSON schema, or EBNF grammar. Pass `so_args={"schema_type": ..., "schema": ...}` to `SamplingParams`; see [examples](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/examples/_structured_output.py).

Supported hardware:

*   NVIDIA SM100 GPUs
*   Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs

Required for a complete inference service (not included in this release):

*   A KV cache system
*   VE/Prefill/Decode disaggregation (most required engine functionality is already implemented)
*   Load balancing across data-parallel replicas for both prefill and decode

## Getting started

### Prerequisites

*   Linux
*   GCC >= 13.0
*   Python 3.12
*   CUDA 13 (NVIDIA only)
*   CANN 9.2 (Ascend only)

### Build from source

Before building DeepInfer, please create and activate an empty Python 3.12 environment.

# Use `ascend` instead for the Ascend platform
# Keep it exported in the environment where you run DeepInfer
export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia
./build.sh

### Offline inference

The default checkpoint, [`deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017`](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017), is downloaded into the Hugging Face cache on the first run; set `DEEPINFER_HF_MODEL_DIR=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017` to run from a local copy instead.

python examples/offline_inference.py

See [examples](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/examples/README.md) for details.

Measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode — each within one scale-up domain. To reproduce the benchmarks, see [run_sweep.sh](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/examples/sweep/run_sweep.sh).

Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car

Google is
bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI
in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search.
As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.”
Google brought its
Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year
before rolling it out to
cars with Google built-in in April
. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps.
Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says.
Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

articles.content:
Title: NixOS is making me less afraid

URL Source: https://entropicthoughts.com/nixos-is-making-me-less-afraid

Markdown Content:
Something funny happened a little while ago: I read about FreshRSS, and it sounded nice, so I _installed it on a server and started using it_. That would not have happened a year ago, but then again, a year ago I didn’t have any NixOS servers.

* * *

For the past few years, my rss feeds have lived locally on my phone only. There was a good idea behind that 1 1 I can mostly take time to read when I’m away from my computer anyway., but it never quite worked in practice. For one, many things are easier to read on a larger screen. But it was also brittle to trust a phone app to manage the read/unread status of thousands of articles across a hundred feeds.2 2 In particular, when I switched to a different phone I could migrate all feeds to it, but the read/unread status was lost along the way. What I really wanted was a server-side feed aggregator. This is software that runs on a server, manages rss feeds, and then I can read the rss feeds either through a web interface, or through client applications. I’ve wanted that for a while, but I’ve never taken the step, because it would be yet another side project to maintain the deployment of.

But now, with some NixOS experience, adding a working FreshRSS configuration (including backups) took 9 lines of Nix code 3 3 Plus a dozen more lines for the nginx reverse proxy configuration. It got a little complicated because I wanted to `proxy_pass` from a specific location block which required rewriting cookie paths. But that’s a me problem, not a NixOS problem.. That installation has just hands-off worked for the past few months. If or when that server breaks, I can spin up a new one running the exact same configuration, probably in something like 15 minutes. When we can do something like that, there is literally no reason to not just try the new software.

Contrast this against how FreshRSS is installed outside of NixOS. Then we’d

1.   download and extract an archive to the right location;
2.   configure permissions according to instructions;
3.   install nginx and php-fpm with necessary extra dependencies to the server;
4.   configure php-fpm pools and make nginx pass requests through to php-fpm;
5.   set up Let’s Encrypt certificates;
6.   set up backups; and
7.   hopefully remember how to do all the above if something breaks and we need to reinstall FreshRSS on a new or upgraded server later.

Of course, the FreshRSS project provides a container image which would shorten the process a little bit. It purports to set up Apache with mod_php and configure them the right way. Then we’d only need to configure backups, create a systemd service that runs the container, and manage nginx as a tls terminating reverse proxy in front of that, because the container image reasonably does not come with tls support. This is still stuff to remember, and there’s also no guarantee the same thing works six months down the line when reinstalling, unless we wrote down which exact container image we downloaded.4 4 It does not help to build the container image from source, because two builds from the same Dockerfile separated by time can result in rather different container images.

* * *

I have mentioned before how much I dislike maintaining side projects. That includes my own code, but also self-hosted services developed by someone else. I’m okay with a few minutes of maintenance here and there, but having to schedule hours of uninterrupted work to upgrade something, or spending _any_ amount of time at all on emergency maintenance, really kills my desire to work with computers.

You’d think someone of my disposition would be deep into configuration management, container orchestration, or both, but no. I have made honest attempts with CFEngine, Ansible, podman, and k3s but none of them improved my installation/configuration/deployment experience significantly over (a) carefully writing things down, and sometimes (b) turning those careful notes into a shell script performing a sequence of `ssh` commands.5 5 Yes, this is essentially reinventing Ansible – but less brittle. It won’t break the next time someone glances sideways at `pip`. The drawback of the shell script is that it often ends up relying on assumptions that become invalid with time, or when it is used in a different environment. A NixOS configuration reads a lot like the careful instructions to myself, except they’re executable and they produce the same result every time.
